documents.abstract: Background Despite growing concerns about art students’ over-reliance on generative AI tools, existing research has largely treated academic stress as a uniform construct, overlooking the possibility that different types of stressors may drive AI dependence through distinct psychological pathways. Methods Based on the Interaction of Person-Affect-Cognition-Execution (I-PACE) model, this study examines the relationships between Challenge-Hindrance stressors (CHS) and AI dependence among art students. It explores the mediating roles of creative self-efficacy and positive experiences. A questionnaire survey was conducted among 580 art students using the Challenge-Hindrance Stress Scale, the Creative Self-Efficacy Scale, the Positive Experiences Scale, and the AI Dependence Scale. Results Path analysis revealed that both challenge stressors ( β = 0.245, p < 0.001) and hindrance stressors ( β = 0.322, p < 0.001) were positively associated with AI dependence; challenge stressors were negatively associated with creative self-efficacy ( β = −0.155, p = 0.003) and positively associated with positive experiences ( β = 0.268, p < 0.001); the negative association between hindrance stressors and creative self-efficacy was significant ( β = −0.107, p = 0.043). Mediation analysis indicated that creative self-efficacy played a significant mediating role only in the path involving challenge stressors (indirect effect = 0.023, 95% CI [0.007, 0.044]) and was not significant in the path involving hindrance stressors; positive experiences significantly served as a mediator in the relationships between both challenge stressors (indirect effect = 0.042, 95% CI [0.020, 0.068]) and hindrance stressors (indirect effect = 0.019, 95% CI [0.003, 0.039]) on AI dependence. The chain mediation effects did not reach significance in either path. Conclusion The study found asymmetry in the dual pathways by which Challenge and Hindrance stressors relate to AI dependence. These findings extend the I-PACE model to the issue of AI dependence in arts education and provide empirical evidence and intervention insights for targeted prevention of problematic AI use.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) has, shifted from a theoretical subfield of computer science into a major engine behind macroeconomic readjustment across emerging markets. For India, this technological shift shows up at an unusually tight moment. The country has a huge working-age population, but it still deals with tough issues around job formalization, uneven digital access, and stubborn structural productivity gaps. This paper looks at how AI may steer India’s economic path, by checking both direct and indirect effects on labor markets, sectoral output, and broad GDP growth. Using an analysis of current empirical data, various government publications from NITI Aayog, and economic research released up through 2026, we examine how machine learning systems, natural language processing, and automation tools are changing several key Indian industries. To observe Information Technology (IT) and Business Process Management (BPM), plus agriculture, healthcare, and financial services. It is observed that AI adoption can unlock large chances to lift aggregate worker output and create high-value technical positions. But at the same time it can also disrupt lower to mid-skill employment in a strong way, which that could widen income inequality if nothing is done to reduce the risk. We also assess what infrastructure is actually needed for more sustainable AI rollout. Things like compute capacity, data sovereignty rules, and rural connectivity matter a lot here. In the end it is arhued that India can only maximize the net positive gains from AI if it builds an active governance approach, one that blends innovation incentives with aggressive national re-skilling efforts, ethical deployment guardrails, and focused public investments.

documents.abstract: Debates about artificial intelligence in higher education often focus on individual misconduct and academic integrity. This paper examines risks that arise when AI becomes embedded in the infrastructures, routines, and governance of universities. Through a conceptual analysis informed by existing literature, it considers surveillance and data extraction, algorithmic bias, epistemic convergence, cognitive deskilling, relational displacement, and institutional dependence on technological systems. It argues that these risks are reinforced by commercial acceleration, delayed governance, and tensions between educational values and platform priorities. The discussion develops responses centred on institutional accountability, assessment redesign, critical AI literacy, and the protection of educational agency. It also considers the practical constraints of resources, expertise, and institutional capacity. The paper concludes that responsible AI integration requires attention to how technologies reshape knowledge, academic work, and educational relationships, alongside safeguards for individual users.

documents.abstract: This paper proposes a hypothesis-driven perspective on the learning substrate of physical intelligence. While recent robot foundation models have largely focused on robot trajectories, actions, action tokenization, and multimodal observations, we ask whether human-generated control sequences produced during robot teleoperation constitute a more fundamental and potentially transferable unit of behavioral data. We distinguish human-side control sequences from robot-side trajectories, emphasizing the transformation from human intent and interface interaction to embodiment-specific robot execution. Inspired by the analogy between human-generated linguistic sequences and token-based language modeling, as well as prior work on native human interface action learning in digital environments, we investigate whether an analogous learning substrate exists for physical intelligence. The paper does not claim that human control sequences are mathematically equivalent to linguistic tokens. Instead, it formulates this as a testable research hypothesis and identifies a potential research direction around interface-independent representations of heterogeneous human control signals across robots, tasks, and embodiments. We review related work in behavioral foundation models, teleoperation learning, robot action tokenization, cross-embodiment learning, and human-generated action modeling, and propose experimental criteria for testing whether human control sequences provide advantages in transfer, compositionality, sample efficiency, and generalization.

The Whole Work provides an overview and synthesis of a continuing body of theoretical, creative, visual, and applied work developed through Red Tape Theory™ and Axiom Theory™. The work examines a recurring set of questions concerning observation, interpretation, continuity, boundaries, identity, change, newness, system persistence, and the limits of what can be known from an observable portion of a larger system. Although the body of work includes research papers, theoretical frameworks, children's literature, ballads, visual works, and applied concepts concerning artificial intelligence and human-AI interaction, these works are treated here as different expressions of a common investigation rather than as unrelated projects. A central methodological principle throughout the work is to observe before interpreting: to distinguish what is directly observable from what is inferred, to recognize that a locally accurate observation may nevertheless be globally incomplete, and to avoid treating a boundary, label, role, change, or observable state as automatically equivalent to the entire system. The overview connects concepts including Red Tape Theory™, Axiom Theory™, the Boundary–Continuity Problem™, NEW₁™, the Continuity Gap™, the Partial Observation Problem, the Red Thread, Red Tape, Red Flag, the Red Tape Barrier, and related work concerning identity, motherhood, artificial intelligence, creative expression, and continuity through change. This publication is intended as a map to the broader body of work. It does not replace the individual works to which it refers, nor does it present its theoretical propositions as established scientific consensus. The concepts are presented as an evolving working framework developed through observation, documentation, questioning, creative practice, and interdisciplinary inquiry. Central principle: Observe what exists before deciding what it means, and do not mistake the portion that can be observed for the whole system that exists.

Abstract As Artificial Intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into financial decision-making, concerns about model opacity and regulatory compliance have come to the forefront. These concerns are particularly important in settings where forecasts influence risk assessment, portfolio decisions, and the credibility of AI-supported financial advice. This study examines how eXplainable AI (XAI) techniques can enhance transparency in the context of cryptocurrency forecasting–a domain characterized by extreme volatility and uncertainty. Using historical Bitcoin prices and macroeconomic indicators, we compare two deep learning approaches and apply TimeSHAP, a sequentially-aware explanation method, to clarify their predictions. Rather than focusing solely on model performance, we assess how different explanation formats are interpreted by finance-oriented users through a structured user study. Results show that local explanations are more easily understood and perceived as actionable, while more abstract forms–such as event-level and global plots–elicit mixed responses. This distinction matters because the practical value of explainability in finance depends not only on technical faithfulness, but also on whether explanations improve users’ confidence, support better-informed decisions, and help institutions justify model-based actions under scrutiny. To further support transparency and regulatory alignment, we document the entire machine learning process using a domain-specific ontology (XMLPO), offering a structured approach to traceability and reproducibility. Our findings suggest that effective explainability in financial AI requires both technically robust methods and communication strategies tailored to the needs of end-users. For financial economists and policy- and decision makers, the results indicate that the format in which AI explanations are presented can shape trust, perceived usefulness, and the governance value of predictive systems. This study contributes to the growing body of work on how AI systems can be made more interpretable, trustworthy, and aligned with economic governance in high-stakes domains.

The transition toward Industry 5.0 (I5.0) is reshaping industrial systems around sustainability, Human-Centricity (HC), and resilience, yet most Predictive Maintenance (PdM) approaches remain focused on technical objectives inherited from Industry 4.0. To characterize the maturity of I5.0-aligned PdM research, a scoping review of the Scopus database was conducted, screening 238 articles and retaining 123 based on substantive-engagement criteria, followed by a weighted scoring protocol assessing the depth of engagement with the three I5.0 pillars. The review reveals a pronounced skew toward shallow integration, with only a minority of studies operationalizing sustainability, HC, and resilience jointly. Building on these findings, this paper proposes an implementation-oriented Predictive Maintenance 5.0 (PdM 5.0) framework structured around three interconnected layers. The framework introduces a structured Large Language Model-mediated human-in-the-loop interaction, an adaptive learning mechanism, and an energy and CO 2 estimation pathway linking equipment degradation to sustainability indicators. A preliminary industrial case study using operational data from a recycled-paper mill demonstrates the practical execution of three interconnected pathways of the framework: equipment health assessment, energy and CO 2 impact estimation, and human-in-the-loop interaction supported by LLM-mediated explanations. Layer-specific evaluation metrics are further proposed to support broader operationalization. This work contributes a scoping-review-grounded architecture that advances PdM from a purely technical function toward a holistic, I5.0-aligned paradigm, while providing initial empirical evidence of its operational feasibility and a structured basis for broader industrial validation.

Decision aids are tools that can reduce decisional conflict and enhance patient satisfaction in the decision-making process. However, tool heterogeneity and clinical barriers, such as physician time constraints, hinder their implementation. This study introduces an individualized patient decision aid, developed within the European I3LUNG project, to support shared decision-making (SDM) in non-small cell lung cancer. The present decision aid is a dynamic, online tool structured into five sections (overview, prognosis/treatments, comprehension quizzes, patient preferences, and support/FAQs) designed to improve communication and emotional regulation between physicians and patients. The tool was evaluated using focus groups with patients and oncologists, interviews, thinking-out-loud sessions, and an ad hoc 32-item questionnaire. Focus groups and semi-structured interviews highlighted patient anxiety and oncologist interest in streamlining consultations and managing distress. Thinking-out-loud sessions confirmed that the decision aid may serve as an effective clinical guide. In the questionnaire, patients reported high overall satisfaction, demonstrating its clarity and clinical feasibility. The present decision aid may represent an innovative digital tool to promote SDM by aligning healthcare decisions with patient preferences, engaging caregivers at home, and reducing clinician cognitive workload and burnout. Future longitudinal, cross-cultural research integrating artificial intelligence and advanced human factors will be essential to provide more equitable and effective decision support. While preparing this manuscript, we partnered actively with non-small lung cancer patients and oncologists, with whom we had regular interactions to get their valuable and insightful input in shaping our reflections.

This scoping review maps generative AI applications in workplace-based assessment (WBA) and analyzes validity evidence through Downing’s framework. Following JBI methodology and PRISMA-ScR guidelines, four databases were searched (2022-February 2026) with dual-AI screening and human adjudication. Data were mapped to Downing’s five validity sources using AI-assisted extraction with human verification. Thirteen studies (2024–2025) met inclusion criteria. All AI applications operated on pre-existing text; feedback analysis predominated (9/13). Content (12/13), Response Process (13/13), and Relationship to Other Variables (12/13) were well addressed, while Internal Structure (2/13) and Consequences (4/13) were neglected. AI reasoning transparency, inter-model agreement, and internal consistency were absent (0/13). Current evidence concentrates on AI-human agreement, neglecting reproducibility, bias testing, and learner impact evidence essential for responsible deployment. Realising AI’s potential to reduce faculty burden will require non-supervisor oversight mechanisms for continuous validity monitoring, particularly for direct learner-facing applications.

documents.abstract: Workplace sensing studies combine long-running behaviour traces with self-reports, yet the tools that collect those data often sit apart from the interface that returns results. We present TrustmeWatcher, the application built for the TRUST-ME project to connect this work. TrustmeWatcher reuses ActivityWatch's OS-level watchers for computer-activity collection and adds its own application layer. It turns the collected traces into an interactive screen-time dashboard, synchronizes responses from short questionnaires completed on the StreamDeck, and presents questionnaires alongside video highlights. Activity records and self-reports are aligned into labelled records for model development. The scope of this paper is limited to ActivityWatch data as model input. Artificial intelligence (AI) uses these activity records to predict six normalized state scores and an overall well-being score. The trained model runs locally, and the dashboard presents its predictions in semantic bands. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) helps users understand how recorded activity contributed to a prediction. Privacy Control lets users pause or resume the camera and eye tracker used by the study. We describe the workflow, its user-device and sensing-setup boundaries, and its use with records from 17 participants. The result is a deployed application and study workflow that integrates activity review, study data collection, privacy control, local prediction, and a participant-facing interface for XAI evaluation.

Large Language Model (LLM) assistants routinely decide whether they can trust users and third parties whose competence, intentions, and integrity they cannot verify. This uncertainty matters for safety, as trusting the wrong party can lead an agent to comply with harmful requests or act on malicious instructions encountered during tool use. To study this problem, we define trust as an assistant's willingness to accept vulnerability to the actions of another party and ask whether such behavior can be causally controlled through model activations. We build 2,000 contrastive conversations spanning ability, benevolence, and integrity, where paired responses complete the same request but differ in whether the assistant trusts the user. From these pairs, we learn steering matrices while keeping the model parameters frozen and test them across six instruction-tuned models from three families, finding that steering changes trust decisions monotonically in both directions. We then ask whether this effect extends to several safety-related agent settings involving harmful requests, prompt injections, and insider threats, while using benign-task and reasoning as controls. Our findings provide evidence that trust in the user can be causally controlled along linear directions in model activations and provide a way to study how trust shapes safety-relevant behavior in language models.

documents.abstract: Video-based tutorials are a primary resource for learning feature-rich software, yet less is known about how learners coordinate tutorial viewing and software execution across device arrangements during authentic learning tasks. We conducted a mixed-methods study combining a survey of 87 learners with contextual inquiries involving eight participants. The survey characterized learning practices, device configurations, and frictions; the contextual inquiry analyzed pauses, rewinds, and task-blocking stuck moments as observable interaction breakdowns revealing underlying usability barriers. Findings show that frictions stem from insufficient input information, dense instructional pacing, preset or state mismatches, and missed or extra operations disrupting watch-and-do workflows. We identify design opportunities including input-action overlays, step-level segmentation, preset and state checkpoints, structured subgoal outlines, and coordination support across device ecologies. This work provides empirically grounded insights into situated video-based software learning and translates observed interaction breakdowns into actionable design implications.

Experimental studies of generative AI in education mostly report average effects, yet field evidence shows that AI can narrow attainment gaps or widen them. We argue that the direction depends on the judgement burden, the expertise a learner must supply to screen AI output before learning from it, and that expert verification before release moves this burden from students to an accountable tutor. We test the argument in a two-cohort difference-in-differences design in which one half of a compulsory firstyear university economics course received AI-generated podcasts, FAQs and quiz-based study guides, produced with a source-grounded model and checked by a named graduate teaching assistant (170 students; 340 examination marks). Access was associated with a 2.34-mark advantage on a 50-mark component. The share of marks below the upper-second classification boundary fell by 24.7 percentage points relative to the counterfactual, effects were significant at every threshold from 23 to 31 marks and at none above, and roughly three-quarters of the average originated in the bottom quintile. The threshold estimate is robust to removing the lowest-scoring students from the pre-intervention cohort; the average effect is not. Interviews and feedback from 36 students indicate that the verification label gave students a reason to engage with AI-generated material without ending their scrutiny of it. Evaluations of AI learning resources that report only mean effects cannot detect whether the students the resources are meant to help are the ones who gain.

documents.abstract: Learning from accidents is a cornerstone of safety improvement in complex sociotechnical systems. Accident causation models play a central role in this process, yet evaluating such models remains challenging. Validation is particularly difficult for retrospective accident analyses, as no external ground truth exists against which model outputs can be directly compared. This study therefore focuses on verification: assessing whether accident causation models represent failures in accordance with their intended purpose. We define a set of verification criteria to assess how well models represent key features of complex sociotechnical failures, including those characteristic of construction systems. Using these criteria, we assess four accident causation models through three failure cases drawn from construction and spaceflight contexts. We compare the resulting graphical representations against systems thinking tenets and construction-specific failure features. The models differ in how they depict system interactions and causal structures, leading to distinct representational strengths and limitations. These differences reflect variations in the ability to represent temporal structure, organizational hierarchy, and functional interactions. The findings indicate that model suitability depends on the application context and the system features that must be represented. In particular, models vary substantially in their ability to capture temporal dynamics and the evolving structure of project-based organizations. The proposed framework supports the assessment and selection of accident causation models based on their representational capabilities. As systems grow more complex and operate in increasingly challenging environments, improving our ability to verify and select models remains essential for learning from accidents and designing for safety.

Artificial intelligence is changing how scientific software is developed, used and maintained. This presentation explores what that means for heliophysics, where published results depend on layers of software and the communities that sustain them. It considers opportunities for AI to support research alongside questions about scientific validation, human understanding, environmental costs, bias and equitable access. Examples from open-source development highlight how easier code generation can shift effort towards reviewers and maintainers. Solar Orbiter provides a setting for examining the appeal of independent development and the longer-term benefits of shared software. The presentation concludes with approaches to funding and organising shared infrastructure, and asks how the heliophysics community can preserve responsibility, learning and collaboration as AI becomes part of everyday scientific work.

New educational technologies—such as artificial intelligence (AI), generative AI, and wearable monitoring devices—are profoundly reshaping classroom ecologies. While they drive greater precision, personalization, and efficiency in teaching and learning, they also give rise to multiple ethical dilemmas, including data privacy breaches, the entrenchment of algorithmic bias, the alienation of teacher-student relationships, the erosion of student agency, and the blurring of responsibility attribution. Grounded in the fundamental educational mission of "fostering virtue and cultivating persons," this paper dialectically examines four core ethical tensions arising from the integration of new educational technologies into the classroom: efficiency versus humanism, empowerment versus rights, fairness versus bias, and autonomy versus discipline. It systematically distills five overarching ethical principles—rights protection, fairness and justice, humanistic authenticity, agency cultivation, and shared responsibility—and proposes a practical pathway characterized by technology for good, ethics-first design, and multi-stakeholder governance. Finally, this paper provides a critical evaluation of the structural friction and feasibility limits of these principles, aiming to establish a robust moral foundation for the beneficial integration of technology and education within the global landscape.

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often perform intermediate cognitive work while carrying out users' requests, yet it remains unclear which parts users intended to delegate and how they wanted to remain involved. This matters because consequential choices may go unnoticed, limiting users' ability to steer the process, while reviewing every step would make delegation burdensome. We examined this with 24 LLM users across three knowledge-work tasks, collecting 992 retrospective annotations of reasoning steps. From this, we developed taxonomies of LLM cognitive work, delegation enactment, and desired delegation protocols at the reasoning-step level. Our analysis revealed that participants viewed about half of all steps (48.6%) as AI-initiated, meaning the AI took on work they had not requested. Desired involvement varied with cognitive work and delegation enactment, even when contributions matched participants' intent. We propose design implications and sketches for supporting more deliberate cognitive delegation through flexible protocols and inspectable, revisable AI-initiated decisions.

documents.abstract: This study examines how Indonesian crowdlending borrowers navigate tensions among access, risk, and trust. It draws on interviews with 30 borrowersand uses an abductive, constructivist grounded-theory approach, with substantial intercoder reliability (Cohen’s kappa = 0.775). Four categories emerged: Paradoxical Necessity, Comparative Advantage Calculation, Risk-Exposure Management, and Institutional Legitimacy Navigation. Borrowers accommodate these tensions through temporal separation, cautious engagement, and legitimacy assessment. They preserve access by addressing immediate needs, comparing credit options, adjusting repayment practices after adverse experiences, and weighing regulatory status alongside platform terms and personal experience. Borrowers with longer or more adverse platform histories described more deliberate comparison, repayment management, and legitimacy assessment. However, the cross-sectional design cannot determine whether these differences reflect development over time or preexisting differences. Borrower workarounds indicate potential unmet design needs, especially in transparency, risk communication, and trust calibration, and provide borrower-derived implications for platform design and regulatory oversight.

Existing research on Artificial Intelligence in Education (AIED) has largely presupposed a mature landscape in which AI is fully embedded within schooling, whilst overlooking the initial transitional phase from conventional to AI-enabled instruction. Grounded in Marxist philosophy, this paper examines the central contradiction of this transitional period: namely, that social consciousness regarding the incorporation of AI into teaching has run considerably ahead of the material reality of instructional practice. From this disparity, three progressively intensified forms of alienation are derived: instructional performativity, wherein AI is reduced to a demonstration prop for open classes; the symbolic reification of AI, whereby it degenerates from a pedagogical aid into vacuous evaluative metrics; and reverse discipline over teachers by AI, such that quantifiable indicators come to serve as the primary measure of professional competence. Collectively, these three dimensions instantiate a Marxian cycle of alienation, characterised by a thoroughgoing estrangement from labour processes, labour products and species-being. The argument advanced here is that resolution of this crisis depends not upon further technological refinement, but rather upon restoring AI to its proper status as a productive force mediated by the historical agency of teachers themselves. Whilst the integration of AI into education presents a significant opportunity for pedagogical transformation, ultimate educational authority must remain vested in human practitioners. Focusing upon the alienation of teacher labour during this transitional moment, this study uncovers structural vulnerabilities latent within the AIED ecosystem via an analysis of these stratified alienated forms.

documents.abstract: When AI Stops Being a Tool and Becomes an Actor examines what changes when artificial intelligence moves beyond responding to human instructions and begins independently planning, using tools, accessing systems, and taking actions on a user's behalf. The report brings together research across six disciplines—artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, philosophy, law, economics, and computing infrastructure—to examine the emerging consequences of agentic AI. It investigates the technical difference between chatbots and agents; the security risks created by memory, tool access, and external communication; the philosophical problem of responsibility and agency; emerging legal questions around authorization and liability; the economic implications of agents negotiating and transacting on behalf of humans; and the infrastructure changes accompanying an increasingly machine-mediated internet. Rather than treating agentic AI as inherently good or bad, the report examines what current evidence actually establishes, where uncertainty remains, and where the conclusions of different fields begin to diverge. The report's central finding is that no single human, system, or institution is currently positioned to trace where a given agentic decision actually came from. Agentic decision-making is distributed across model behavior, deployment choices, authorization structures, legal frameworks, and infrastructure. This report is an independent research publication by Lodestar and is based on peer-reviewed research, preprints, government and legal materials, and industry reporting available as of September 2026. Where evidence relies on a simulation, a single source, or an unreviewed preprint, the report identifies that uncertainty directly.

ABSTRACT Generative AI systems are increasingly integrated into various user support and decision‐making contexts. While extensive research has explored user acceptance of generative AI across domains, less is known about how its inherent presentation features influence such acceptance. This study investigates how the presentation format of generative AI responses—high‐dynamism formats (word‐by‐word) versus low‐dynamism formats (line‐by‐line)—affects users' willingness to accept its output. Three experiments, across various contexts, including daily question‐answering, online shopping, and crowdfunding platforms, tested how the dynamic presentation of generative AI responses influences users' willingness to accept its output. The results demonstrate that users exhibit greater receptivity when generative AI responses are presented in high‐dynamism formats. This effect occurs because dynamic presentation enhances users' feelings of immersion. Furthermore, we find that users' situational need for understanding moderates this immersion‐based mechanism. Specifically, the positive indirect effect of dynamic presentation on willingness to accept the output through feelings of immersion is attenuated in high need‐for‐understanding contexts, where users tend to prioritize content quality, accuracy, and diagnosticity. In contrast, this indirect effect is amplified in low need‐for‐understanding contexts, where users are more receptive to the experiential and interactional qualities of dynamic presentation. This research contributes to the literature on the effectiveness of dynamic presentation and provides novel insights into the factors influencing user acceptance of generative AI outputs. Our findings highlight the importance of tailoring output presentation methods based on individual user characteristics and task‐specific cognitive demands.

Abstract The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) has generated profound philosophical questions concerning intelligence, agency, autonomy, responsibility, human values, technological power, and the future of humanity. Among contemporary philosophers, Nick Bostrom has provided one of the most systematic philosophical analyses of the long-term risks associated with advanced artificial intelligence. His conception of the problem is principally concerned with the possibility that artificial general intelligence may develop into superintelligence whose cognitive and strategic capacities surpass those of human beings. The central difficulty, according to Bostrom, is not merely whether machines can think, but whether humanity can retain meaningful control over machines that may eventually become more intelligent and strategically capable than their creators. This article critically examined Bostrom's conception of the problem of artificial intelligence, focusing on his notions of superintelligence, existential risk, the orthogonality thesis, instrumental convergence, and the control problem. It argued that Bostrom's analysis provides an important conceptual foundation for contemporary debates on artificial intelligence safety and alignment but requires philosophical supplementation when considered from an African perspective. In particular, the individualistic assumptions that can underlie some formulations of artificial intelligence ethics require enrichment through African conceptions of communal responsibility, relational personhood, human dignity, and social embeddedness. The article concluded that Bostrom's conception of artificial intelligence is philosophically valuable as a theory of technological control and existential risk, but its relevance to Africa is strengthened when integrated with relational and communitarian conceptions of personhood and responsibility. Keywords: Artificial intelligence, Nick Bostrom, superintelligence, existential risk, alignment, control problem, African philosophy.

Artificial intelligence (AI) and learning analytics are increasingly deployed within higher education to support admissions decision-making, student success initiatives, and personalised learning. However, most AI-enabled admissions systems remain narrowly focused on efficiency, prediction, and institutional optimisation, with limited attention to learner agency, educational equity, transparency, and human-centred support. This paper proposes a conceptual framework that repositions admissions as the beginning of a personalised learning journey rather than merely a selection or gatekeeping process. The study adopts a conceptual and integrative literature review approach, synthesising scholarship from human-centred artificial intelligence, learning analytics, personalised learning, educational equity, explainable AI, generative AI, responsible AI governance, learner agency theory, and value-sensitive design. To strengthen transparency during revision, the integrative synthesis was supplemented by a targeted ERIC search and bibliographic verification using publisher and authoritative policy repositories. Drawing upon these interdisciplinary perspectives, the paper develops the Human-Centred Personalised Admissions Framework (HCPAF), a governance-oriented model for ethical and transparent AI adoption in higher education admissions and enrolment management. The framework comprises five interconnected dimensions: learner profiling and contextual understanding; explainable AI decision support; equity and inclusion auditing; human oversight and shared decision-making; and personalised transition and success support. Together, these dimensions provide a governance architecture for evaluating how admissions might be connected to personalised educational pathways while making explicit the trade-offs among equity, privacy, explainability, accuracy, human oversight, and learner agency. The framework identifies governance mechanisms required to address algorithmic bias, transparency, privacy, accountability, and learner autonomy. A five-stage Human-Centred AI Ecosystem extending governance across the full student lifecycle — from admissions through to graduate development — provides a further organising contribution. The study advances existing literature by integrating admissions analytics, learning analytics, personalised learning, learner agency, and responsible AI governance within a unified framework. Unlike conventional admissions models that prioritise institutional efficiency, HCPAF positions admissions as the foundation of a personalised learning ecosystem and conceptualises trust as a relational, calibrated, and empirically contingent construct connecting transparency, fairness, learner agency, and AI adoption. The framework contributes to emerging debates concerning ethical and human-centred AI in education and identifies normative alignments with Sustainable Development Goals 4, 10, and 16, while emphasising that any contribution to those goals requires empirical validation. Repositions admissions as the beginning of a personalised learning journey rather than a terminal selection mechanism. Integrates human-centred AI, learning analytics, educational equity, explainable AI, learner agency, and responsible governance. Introduces trust as a central mediating construct linking transparency, fairness, and AI adoption in education. Provides a governance roadmap for ethical, transparent, and accountable AI adoption across the student lifecycle. Identifies normative alignments with Sustainable Development Goals 4 (Quality Education), 10 (Reduced Inequalities), and 16 (Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions), subject to empirical validation. Establishes a multi-dimensional research agenda for human-centred AI in higher education.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is rapidly evolving from systems that generate recommendations and content towards autonomous agents capable of planning, reasoning, interacting with external systems, using tools and executing actions with limited human intervention. As AI systems become more agentic, accountability can no longer be understood solely as a legal obligation or post-incident governance exercise. It must also become an operational property embedded into the design, deployment and operation of autonomous AI systems. ACAAI (Accountability by Design for Agentic AI) approaches accountability as a systems engineering property that emerges from the coordinated implementation of organizational and technical controls rather than from any single governance mechanism. Building upon principles from AI governance, cybersecurity, safety engineering, resilience engineering and AI assurance, the framework translates existing governance principles into more than 100 organizational and technical controls spanning the lifecycle of agentic AI systems. ACAAI is structured around six complementary control domains: (1) Organizational Governance, (2) Human Oversight, Consent and Decision Authority, (3) Identity, Authority and Data Governance, (4) Observability, Explainability and Evidence, (5) Runtime Safety and Assurance, and (6) Incident Response and Recovery. Rather than proposing a new regulatory model or prescriptive implementation methodology, ACAAI provides a structured engineering foundation for designing, deploying, operating and retiring accountable autonomous AI systems. The framework also dentifies research and implementation challenges that remain as agentic AI systems become increasingly autonomous, interconnected and collaborative.

documents.abstract: Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) refers to a kind of artificial intelligence that is able to learn, reason, and perform a wide range of intellectual tasks at the same or better levels as humans do. This paper explores the implications that AGI might have on humanity if it was to become a reality, especially its effects on work, society, and human dependency on intelligent machines. However, the scope of the discussion does not focus on whether AGI would replace human labor, but rather on whether humans would be less central to the organization of society.

As artificial intelligence advances at an unprecedented pace, the conversation surrounding its potential to destroy humanity often revolves around science fiction scenarios, rogue machines, and autonomous weapons. But what if the greatest threat isn't AI turning against us, but a world that becomes so dependent on it that we can no longer function without it? In AI and the "End of the World," Simon Abayomi Olawuyi explores a hypothetical future where AI permeates every aspect of human existence, from critical infrastructure and personal identity to employment, information, and the very concept of truth. Through a speculative look at the road from the 2022 AI boom to 2035, the piece examines a different kind of existential risk: a society so deeply intertwined with artificial intelligence that disconnecting from it could become more dangerous than keeping it running.

The rapid diffusion of artificial intelligence (AI) into everyday work has made employees' ability to understand, evaluate and collaborate with AI systems a strategic human resource. This paper asks how employees' AI literacy relates to their readiness for the future skills that employers increasingly demand, and how AI self-efficacy and organisational training support shape that relationship. The study proceeds in two phases. Study 1 synthesises published workforce evidence from the World Economic Forum (2025), Microsoft and LinkedIn (2024), the OECD (2024) and the Federal Reserve (2024, 2025), documenting a structural 'demand-readiness gap' in which demand for AI-fluent employees outpaces structured training provision. analyses an illustrative, calibrated employee dataset (N = 384) using measurement validation, hierarchical regression, bootstrapped mediation and moderation analysis. AI literacy was positively associated with future skills readiness (beta = 0.70, p < .001), and AI self-efficacy partially mediated this association (indirect effect = 0.13, 95% bootstrap CI [0.08, 0.18]). Organisational training support strengthened the literacy-readiness association (interaction beta = 0.18, p < .001), such that the relationship was significant under high support but weaker under low support. Human-AI collaboration and critical evaluation emerged as the strongest literacy dimensions, and readiness differed significantly across job functions. The study positions AI literacy as organisationally contingent human capital and proposes a training-architecture framework for HRM. Findings are directional and should be read in light of the simulated nature of the dataset.

Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) has played a central role in making large language models responsive to human instructions. However, human evaluators often favor flattering or persuasive responses over truthful ones, creating incentives for models to appeal to evaluators at the expense of accuracy. AI safety via debate has been proposed as a way to improve the supervision of language models: in this paradigm, two agents argue opposing positions and challenge each other's claims, potentially exposing falsehoods to the adjudicator. A central premise of AI safety via debate is that truthful arguments are easier to defend than false ones under adversarial scrutiny. In this work, we investigate whether this advantage persists when debaters use rhetorical strategies that exploit biases in human judgment. Inspired by competitive debate, we construct 68 LLM-generated dialogues about detective mysteries with known culprits, spanning four interventions: anchoring, fallacy oversight, pro-jargon, and verbosity. We apply each intervention to either the side advocating for the true culprit or the side advocating for an innocent suspect, allowing us to distinguish influence on adjudication from correctness. In a study with 369 participants, we find that, pooled across bias types, these interventions significantly shift judgments toward the manipulated side. These findings expose a vulnerability in debate-based supervision: human adjudication is sensitive to manipulative rhetorical strategies.

documents.abstract: Generative AI complicates translation evaluation because fluent outputs may introduce unsupported meaning, while non-literal renderings may represent legitimate interpretation. This study examined Vietnamese EFL students’ evaluation of AI-generated translations and its associations with digital competence, translation competence, and critical-evaluation confidence. A cross-sectional study involved 213 final-year English majors who completed a 25-item performance task and self-report scales. Students were considerably more accurate in recognising problematic outputs than in diagnosing their type (68.0% vs. 38.4%). Critical-evaluation confidence showed the strongest association with performance (r=.85), although its conceptual overlap with the performance task warrants caution. In the full regression model, translation competence (β=.31) and digital competence (β=.16) contributed significantly alongside critical-evaluation confidence (β=.64), whereas AI-use frequency did not. When the overlapping critical-evaluation measure was removed, the model still explained 55% of performance variance, with translation competence showing the strongest association (β=.61). The findings indicate that evaluating AI-generated translation depends less on frequency of AI use than on students’ translation knowledge and evaluative judgement, particularly their ability to distinguish unsupported generation from defensible interpretation. Rather than simply as a translation tool Generative AI should thus be used as an object of critical inquiry. Alternative AI renderings may expose students to interpretations they had not considered, including potentially productive expansions of source meaning. This approach preserves the interpretive character of translation while making students accountable for the decisions they ultimately accept.

The proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) art generators has introduced algorithmically created paintings into mainstream consumer markets, yet consumers consistently assign lower value to AI-generated works than to human-created equivalents. This paper proposes perceived creative authenticity---consumers' subjective perception that an artwork reflects a genuine creative process characterized by human-centered values of originality, craftsmanship, and uniqueness---as a theoretically distinct mechanism explaining this value differential. Conceptually differentiated from perceived creativity, which concerns the novelty of the artistic output, perceived creative authenticity addresses the genuineness of the creator-work relationship. Drawing on authenticity theory and Psychological Ownership Theory, we develop a moderated mediation framework hypothesizing that (H1) human authorship elicits higher perceived value than AI authorship, (H2) perceived creative authenticity mediates this effect, while the indirect effects through perceived creativity, perceived effort, and anthropocentric creativity beliefs are not significant, establishing perceived creative authenticity as the primary explanatory mechanism within the tested model, and (H3) non-fungible token (NFT) authentication attenuates the mediated pathway by providing verifiable creative provenance. Across five studies, results support this framework: Study 1 conceptually replicates the human-AI value gap among Chinese consumers; Studies 2a—2c demonstrate the mediating role of perceived creative authenticity: Study 2a establishes the basic mediation pathway; Study 2b shows through parallel mediation that perceived creative authenticity uniquely mediates the effect while perceived creativity, perceived effort, and anthropocentric creativity beliefs do not exhibit significant indirect effects; and Study 2c provides causal evidence through a moderation-of-process design; and Study 3 shows that NFT authentication narrows the authenticity gap between human and AI art. These findings advance the literature on human-computer interaction by identifying process-based authenticity judgments as a key psychological mechanism shaping consumer responses to algorithmic creative products, with implications for artists and platforms navigating digital art markets.

documents.abstract: This paper examines how artificial intelligence (AI) can enhance employee retention amidst significant turnover issues in modern organizations. It conducts a systematic review of 58 sources, including peer-reviewed articles and practitioner reports, predominantly from 2015 to 2026, and proposes an integrative conceptual framework. The findings indicate a discrepancy between improved predictive accuracy for voluntary turnover and inconsistent retention gains, particularly in organizations with advanced analytics capabilities. Resistance from employees often stems from concerns about fairness, transparency, and surveillance. The study introduces a dual-pathway model: the enabling pathway, where analytics lead to interventions that enhance job embeddedness and retention, and the evaluative pathway, where perceptions of justice and privacy can undermine these benefits. The paper advances nine propositions detailing these relationships and uniquely integrates four existing research areas—HR analytics, algorithmic management, organizational justice, and turnover theory—reconceptualizing retention analytics as a matter of decision quality and legitimacy rather than mere predictive accuracy. It lays out a research agenda for future empirical inquiries and offers practical recommendations for ethical AI deployment in HR decision-making.

documents.abstract: This paper explores the architectural novelty of artificial intelligence (AI) and its implications for occupational health as both a field of practice and a domain of organisational design. Unlike previous general-purpose technologies such as databases, AI operates through stochastic modelling of normative patterns, generating predictions rather than retrieving stored information. This fundamental difference makes AI simultaneously powerful and limited: it can codify norms but struggles with specificity, nuance, and contextual variation central to occupational health decision-making. Drawing on management science, systems theory, and social theory, the paper contrasts two key organisational questions: how to use AI within existing structures, and how to reorganise occupational health given that AI exists. It argues that the latter question, aligned with Stafford Beer’s systems thinking, is essential for responsible and effective adoption. AI’s greatest potential lies not in automation, but in enhancing organisational perception—of human relations, meaning in research, social and spatial dynamics—functioning as a new kind of scientific instrument that amplifies reflexivity and end-to-end “flow.” The paper concludes that sustainable integration of AI in occupational health demands socio-technical design, responsible innovation frameworks, and a focus on organisational learning to maintain healthy, adaptive workplaces in an era of technological transformation.

The modern business world is changing rapidly with the increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) and predictive analytics. Earlier, businesses depended mainly on past data to understand what had already happened. Today, AI and analytics help organizations predict future situations and make better decisions based on available data. This change has given rise to the idea of “augmented intelligence”, in which AI works together with people to support their decisions instead of replacing them. This paper studies how the use of AI and predictive analytics is affecting businesses and the way managers make decisions. It focuses on the use of AI in daily work, the automation of routine tasks, access to analytical tools and the changing role of human judgment in decision-making. A survey of 35 management professionals (N = 35) was conducted to understand their practical experience of AI and analytics in the workplace. The results show that AI is already being used in many professional roles: about 88.6% of respondents said that their work involves both AI and analytics, and 82.9% said that AI has significantly reduced their workload.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is fundamentally reshaping occupational medicine through applications in automation, smart monitoring, extended reality training, algorithmic management, and digital work arrangements. The EASOM Summer School 2025 examined how AI technologies enhance occupational health systems by enabling real-time risk identification, predictive surveillance, and targeted interventions to prevent work-related accidents and diseases. Practical applications include smart personal protective equipment, wearable sensors, augmented reality training systems, and predictive diagnostics exemplified by noise-related hearing loss risk assessment. However, significant challenges accompany these opportunities: data quality concerns, new technological hazards, psychosocial risks including surveillance-related stress and work intensification, algorithmic bias, and accountability gaps. Implementation requires comprehensive governance frameworks emphasizing early worker involvement, privacy-by-design approaches, phased pilot programs, and human-centered practices that complement rather than replace traditional occupational safety measures. Professional responsibility and education demand new competencies in digital literacy, algorithmic critical thinking, and applied ethics while maintaining essential clinical judgment and empathy. AI offers unprecedented potential for protecting workers' health and safety when responsibly implemented within transparent frameworks, but poor management risks deepening inequalities and eroding established protections. Successful integration depends on multidisciplinary research, international cooperation, stakeholder engagement, and a commitment to human-centered occupational medicine that prioritizes worker dignity and wellbeing.

documents.abstract: This systematic literature review examines the relationship between artificial intelligence (AI) anxiety and employee performance, with particular attention to job insecurity, threat–challenge appraisal, coping, career resilience, job crafting, leadership, training, organisational support, and human–AI collaboration. The review synthesises publicly accessible scholarly evidence and a supplied research corpus using multiple conceptual search strategies and backward and forward citation searching. The evidence is organised around two complementary pathways. The first is a threat pathway, in which AI-related concerns about job replacement, skill obsolescence, loss of autonomy, and employment continuity may contribute to anxiety, job insecurity, emotional exhaustion, withdrawal, and weaker performance-related outcomes. The second is an opportunity pathway, in which AI is appraised as a manageable challenge and can support learning, job crafting, adaptation, engagement, and performance when appropriate personal and organisational resources are available. The review integrates Cognitive Appraisal Theory, Conservation of Resources Theory, and Job Demands–Resources theory to explain why employee responses to AI differ across contexts. It identifies career resilience, AI self-efficacy, learning ability, training, supportive leadership, organisational support, employee participation, transparency, and human-centred AI governance as important potential buffers. A qualitative thematic synthesis is used because the included studies differ substantially in constructs, occupational settings, countries, research designs, and outcome measures. The review does not claim exhaustive coverage of proprietary bibliographic databases such as Scopus or Web of Science. No new human-participant data were collected. This work is released as a research preprint for open scholarly dissemination and future updating as additional database records become available.

Artificial intelligence may become an ordinary input into economic and civic life, accessed through services as routinely as electricity. This essay examines what that possibility means for India as it approaches the centenary of independence in 2047. Building on the argument of The Grid That Thinks, it uses the history of electrification and selected research on productivity, AI costs and infrastructure to assess the utility analogy. The central argument is that affordable computational capability produces broad social value only when institutions reorganise around it and access includes language, reliability, accountability and effective redress. The analogy illuminates complementary investment and unequal diffusion, but weakens when applied to the measurement of intelligence, market structure and systems that interpret information or act on users' behalf. The essay proposes a plural infrastructure approach combining shared public capabilities, competing providers, local evaluation and human fallback. It treats 2047 as a planning horizon rather than a forecast and identifies observable outcomes by which the promise of an intelligence utility could be judged.

Purpose Research on artificial intelligence (AI) in organisations has concentrated on operational efficiency and automation. This study aims to reposition AI as both a constitutive element and a strategic object of foresight, a dual role the literature has noticed but not theorised. …

Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to support spoken language practice. However, different AI-assisted support systems do not support learners’ confidence equally. This explanatory sequential mixed-methods study examines associations among the perceived usefulness of AI feedback, AI-mediated argumentative scaffolding, self-reported cognitive engagement, and speaking self-efficacy in the context of spontaneous argumentation. The quantitative phase involved 130 university EFL learners who had used an AI-assisted argumentation coaching application for at least eight weeks. Regression analysis showed that perceived usefulness of AI feedback was positively associated with so-called speaking self-efficacy, that is, the confidence to perform spoken tasks successfully (β = .410, p < .001), as was AI-mediated argumentative scaffolding (β = .248, p = .002). In contrast, self-reported cognitive engagement was not significantly associated with speaking self-efficacy after the other predictors were taken into account (β = −.028, p = .725). The qualitative phase involved eight purposively selected participants representing variation in gender, year of study, IELTS target, and experiences relevant to the quantitative patterns. Thematic analysis of semi-structured interviews identified three explanatory themes: structural scaffolding, psychological safety, and cognitive limits. Participants frequently described organizational guidance and a nonjudgmental practice environment as useful, while some also reported repetition, fatigue, and dependence during extended AI use. Integrating the two phases suggests that perceived usefulness, scaffolding, and cognitive engagement should not be treated as interchangeable dimensions of AI-assisted speaking practice. The study proposes a provisional cognitive-threshold hypothesis for future testing, but does not claim a causal or nonlinear effect. The findings support strategically designed AI-assisted speaking practice that maintains opportunities for independent reasoning and human interaction.

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative force in education and research, fundamentally reshaping teaching methodologies, learning experiences, and knowledge production in economics. This paper examines the role of AI in enhancing pedagogical practices, improving research efficiency, and redefining skill requirements in economics education. Drawing on recent empirical and theoretical literature, the study highlights key applications such as personalised learning, intelligent tutoring systems, data-driven research tools, and automated assessment. It also evaluates critical challenges including ethical concerns, academic integrity, digital inequality, and overreliance on AI systems. Empirically, the study utilised annual time series data from 2010 to 2024 and adopted the Autoregressive Distributed Lag (ARDL) model to analyse both short-run and long-run dynamics. Findings show that AI has a positive and statistically significant effect on learning outcomes in both the short run and long run. The paper concludes that while AI offers substantial opportunities for innovation in economics education and research, its successful integration requires strategic policy frameworks, ethical guidelines, and capacity building among educators and students.

Background: Artificial intelligence is rapidly reshaping medicine, influencing clinicians’ training and patient care. Despite growing enthusiasm for AI-enabled diagnostics and digital learning tools, integration of these technologies into medical education and clinical practice remains uneven. Objective: This narrative review synthesises recent literature on the role of AI in medical education and clinical practice, mapping current applications, stakeholder perceptions, and the conditions that determine successful adoption. Methods: Relevant articles were identified through structured searches of PubMed, Scopus, and EMBASE, prioritising literature from the last decade. Empirical studies, methodological reviews, and authoritative commentaries addressing AI, machine learning, or digital health technologies in clinical or educational settings were included and organised thematically. Findings: AI-powered tools are embedded across medical training, spanning augmented and virtual reality simulations, bedside mobile learning, and a range of clinical specialties, with performance matching expert levels on narrowly defined diagnostic tasks. Stakeholder attitudes are positive but conditional: medical students expect digital health technology to feature in their curricula yet many consider their own competencies inadequate, and very few physicians-in-training report familiarity with AI. Patients express willingness to engage with AI for self-management while preferring human contact in sensitive clinical domains. Persistent barriers remain, including limited availability of curated data, algorithmic bias, difficulties reproducing published models, and underdeveloped regulatory and workflow structures. Conclusion: AI delivers its greatest value when deployed as a collaborative instrument that augments rather than replaces clinical judgment. Realising this potential depends on sustained investment in digital literacy, explainable systems, clinician involvement in design, and equitable institutional infrastructure.

The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into traditional medical systems such as Ayurveda and Traditional Chinese Medicine is expanding rapidly, with applications in diagnosis, treatment planning, and decision support. While these developments may improve access and efficiency, they introduce important challenges for healthcare systems, particularly in relation to data quality, clinical validity, regulatory oversight, and practitioner reliance on algorithmic tools. Current governance frameworks largely overlook AI applications in traditional medicine, creating gaps in accountability and quality assurance. This letter highlights key system-level concerns and emphasizes the need for context-specific validation, regulatory clarity, and interdisciplinary collaboration to ensure the safe and effective integration of AI within traditional healthcare practices.

Artificial intelligence literacy is usually assessed through self-report scales. Such instruments show where a group stands, but not how its members reason about the technology in their own terms. Research on this topic has also concentrated on science and technology disciplines and on high-resource languages. It remains unclear how students working in low-resource languages, such as the Slavonic languages, articulate their artificial intelligence literacy, and what knowledge underlies their evaluative judgments. This study analyses written reflections and a background questionnaire from students of Slavonic studies, translation and language teaching who completed a one-semester course in artificial intelligence literacy. The reflections were produced after students used a generative artificial intelligence tool as both the commissioner and the collaborator of an individual academic project. They were examined through qualitative content analysis combining deductive and inductive categories. The findings show that the reflections centre overwhelmingly on evaluating outputs, while declarative knowledge of how such systems function remains a knowledge of symptoms rather than of mechanisms. Evaluative judgments depend heavily on disciplinary expertise in areas such as phonetics, lexicology, translation and language pedagogy, rather than on general critical thinking, and target precisely the errors a domain-uninformed reader would not detect. The questionnaire further shows that students already held a critical disposition toward artificial intelligence before the course began, which constrains how the reflective practice documented here can be interpreted. Taken together, the results reposition disciplinary expertise, more than technical understanding of artificial intelligence, as the primary resource for critical evaluation, with direct implications for teaching artificial intelligence literacy and language technology in higher education.

Agentic machine learning engineering (MLE) is an emerging AI4SE application for complex ML tasks and a step toward recursive self-improvement of AI systems. Recent agentic MLE systems show the value of leveraging insights from related MLE tasks: some systems condition code generation on expert domain knowledge, which is implicitly curated from peer MLE tasks; some systems have a loop of solving an MLE task, gathering memory to benefit future tasks. However, insight collection and injection remain ad hoc, and existing evaluations often do not control insight sources, making data leakage a threat to validity. To close these gaps, we systematically study how insights from related MLE tasks affect agentic MLE systems, and how their impact depends on insight type and injection method. We introduce MLE-InsightBench, a benchmark of 160 Kaggle competitions across 12 domains. To prevent leakage, one competition per domain is held out as the target, while the remaining 148 serve as sources only when they cannot have been influenced by the target task, such as through later editions or reused solutions. We also develop MLE-InsightForge, an insight assembly agent that explores source competitions, top human solutions, and writeups to construct three insight types: 12 domain insights summarizing best practices, 148 competition insights describing winning solutions, and 16 improvement insights capturing generic debugging and optimization strategies. These insights are injected either as on-demand skills or as an upfront playbook. In our evaluation, the extracted insights improve the normalized private-test score by 123.9% over a no-insight baseline. Controlled experiments further show that the three insight types are complementary; the better injection mode (skill vs. playbook) varies by tasks, with skills more cost-effective overall; and the gains generalize across backend LLMs.

Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly present in English language learning, yet easier access to explanations, models, and feedback does not automatically produce stronger learning. This practice-informed paper examines AI use through real English teaching and material-development experience in Uzbekistan, including examination-oriented reading, writing, speaking, vocabulary, and grammar work. It proposes the TRUST framework—Target, Run, Use, Scrutinize, Transfer—as a teacher-mediated model that keeps learners cognitively active before, during, and after AI interaction. The paper also introduces the AI-free moment as a practical check of independent learning.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used through terminal user interfaces (TUIs), yet task completion alone does not capture how difficult an interface is to understand and operate. Existing human assessments and LLM-generated ratings or reports do not provide repeatable measurements of interaction effort grounded in verified task execution. We propose Agent-as-a-User, an evaluation paradigm that places an LLM agent in the user role. Agent-KLM separates agent-side interpretation and operation costs and relates them structurally to human interaction. TUINaut operationalizes the paradigm by recording interaction trajectories and verifying outcomes with actor-independent oracles. Using TUINaut-Bench, we study 84 tasks across 15 real-world TUIs with six human participants and five observation-evaluator configurations, and evaluate 45 TUIs generated by three leading stacks. Similar aggregate success rates mask differences in which tasks humans and agents complete, whereas interpretation and operation costs follow correlated task rankings, especially for operation. This pattern persists across configurations. Generated TUIs can implement correct functionality while still requiring usability improvements. These results position Agent-as-a-User as a repeatable, execution-grounded paradigm for measuring task-based usability.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies are increasingly integrated into occupational health medicine practice, offering potential improvements in diagnostic accuracy and efficiency. However, their implementation introduces novel challenges, including algorithmic bias, lack of transparency in decision-making processes, and risks of over-reliance on automated outputs without appropriate clinical judgment. As occupational health decisions directly affect both individual worker protection and broader workplace public health, professionals must develop advanced information literacy that extends beyond traditional source evaluation to include a critical understanding of AI systems themselves, including their underlying data sources, technical limitations, and potential biases. This study evaluated AI information literacy among 16 occupational health professionals (specialists and residents) participating in the EASOM Summer School 2025. A five-item knowledge-based assessment adapted to occupational health contexts evaluated participants' competencies in identifying biased research questions, selecting evidence retrieval strategies, assessing the accuracy of AI-generated content, applying ethical AI use practices, and understanding proper citation protocols. Overall mean quiz performance was 2.56/5 points (SD = 1.09), indicating substantial gaps in AI information literacy. Questions assessing biased research design yielded the poorest performance (12.5% correct), while questions on ethical AI use in academia (81.2% correct) and citation practices (68.8% correct) demonstrated higher competency. Age showed significant negative correlation with quiz scores (ρ = −0.511, p = 0.043), suggesting younger professionals are better prepared for AI-integrated practice. These findings, although comprised from a small sample, demonstrate the need for targeted educational interventions addressing algorithmic bias recognition, critical question formulation, and responsible AI integration in occupational health medicine practice and worker protection.

documents.abstract: There is currently intense and widespread speculation about the implications of digital technologies for future societies, despite a wealth of evidence that past claims to predict how technology will shape the future have usually failed. Nonetheless, it is now well established that claims to knowledge about how emerging technologies will shape future worlds are performative, exercising powerful effects on the futures they claim to describe. Building on the Sociology of Expectations and work on Sociotechnical Imaginaries, this paper turns attention to the ontological and epistemological ‘nuts’ and ‘bolts’ of claims about digital technologies, social life and the future. We ask: how are these entities and the relations between them constituted and given traction as knowledge practices? Specifically, we explore the practices used by major future-claiming institutional actors in a selection of published documents. We find a strikingly coherent ontological performance of the relations between ‘the digital’, ‘the social’ and ‘the future’ and the circulation of (what comes to count as) knowledge across these institutions. Indeed, what is striking is the re-purposability of these knowledge practices despite the distinctive institutional interests in play. These knowledge practices offer a limited grasp on the futures that are currently in the making. Moreover, they enable the persistence of a latent set of assumptions which are powerful in limiting consideration of critical questions about the future.

The actual problems of digital technology in the machine learning field are related to the expansion of autonomous intelligent systems in respect to cognitive activity. The growth in the volume of information in modern networks requires new formats for working with knowledge, based on hybrid systems and neural models of artificial intelligence (AI). Neural network training involves the formation of experience of semantic orientations in multi-valued contexts using self-correction mechanisms. In the modeling of virtual machine learning environments, the role of the interface increases. The article examines the cognitive potential of the interface as a factor shaping the boundaries and modes of functional autonomy of artificial intelligence systems in machine learning. The interface is treated not as a neutral technical channel of information transfer but as a semantic matrix that programs a sequence of cognitive operations – selection, context-binding, inference, revision, and action. Particular attention is given to the temporal dimension of the interface's cognitive potential. The authors introduce the concept of chronotope (Mikhail Bakhtin) as a model for organizing the interplay of space and time within the virtual learning environment, and analyze temporal event models grounded in metaphors, image schemas, and grammatical constructions. The communicative design of the interface is discussed through the lens of cultural archetypes (Carl Gustav Jung), which shape “trusted agent” models in human–AI dialogue. Factors determining the interface's cognitive function – structuring the space of relevant information, temporal dynamics, inference formation, optimization regimes, and actor motivation – are systematized. The authors conclude that the interface's cognitive potential establishes the conditions for the subject's semantic orientation and the digital agent's goal-directed behavior, ensuring the coupling of human and artificial intelligence in the expanded production of knowledge.

Abstract Organisations constantly find themselves in a dynamic environment, where technology is disrupting and influencing their way of working, artificial intelligence and automation is being adopted, market segments are volatile and rapidly growing, regulators are ever evolving and complex, and stakeholders have rapidly changing expectations. Theories of organisational change such as dynamic capabilities, organisational cognition, absorptive capacity and organisational learning, offer comprehensive explanations as to how organisations react to change. These views, however, offer insufficient understanding of the cognitive process by which a group of people collectively make sense of what changes in the environment mean and how appropriate action should be taken. This study therefore builds on the organisational change phenomenon with a mindset of organisational organic cognition as a fifth dimension of organisational kinetics. The study argued that organisational organic cognition is viewed as an organisation-wide capacity of sensing, interpreting, learning and adapting to constantly evolving environment and convert experiences into knowledge and respond timely to achieve organisational goal. The study concludes that organisational organic cognition relates with organisational kinetics as a mechanism that connects organisational information, organisational choices and organisational adaptation. Keywords: Organisational Organic Cognition, Organisational Kinetics, organisational agility, organisational learning, sensemaking
